items.q: Commonest cerebellopontine angle tumour is which?
items.exp: Vestibular (acoustic) schwannoma accounts for roughly 80 percent of angle tumours, arising in the internal meatus from vestibular nerve Schwann cells. Meningioma is second.
r: Incorrect. Meningioma is second commonest.
Correct. Vestibular schwannoma dominates CPA.
Incorrect. Epidermoid is uncommon.
Incorrect. Metastases rarely isolate to angle.
items.kp: Eight in ten angle tumours are schwannomas.

items.q: Pulsatile tinnitus synchronous with pulse and red mass behind drum indicate what?
items.exp: Vascular paraganglioma visible through drum causes pulsatile tinnitus and conductive loss; pressure blanching (Brown sign) supports it. Biopsy is avoided; imaging and embolisation plan treatment.
r: Incorrect. Schwartze blush is faint pink without pulsatile tinnitus mass.
Correct. Glomus tumour until proven otherwise.
Incorrect. Cholesteatoma is white keratin with foul discharge.
Incorrect. Effusion dulls drum without vascular mass.
items.kp: Red drum mass pulsing with heartbeat: glomus, do not biopsy.

items.q: In vestibular schwannoma surgery, outcome prioritised above hearing is what?
items.exp: Facial paralysis devastates eye, face and social function, so facial preservation rates headline surgical series, with hearing preservation attempted only in selected small tumours and favourable approaches.
r: Incorrect. Taste via chorda is minor morbidity.
Correct. Facial function outranks hearing.
Incorrect. Vestibular loss compensates centrally usually.
Incorrect. Tinnitus often persists despite surgery.
items.kp: Save the face first in angle surgery.

items.q: MRI dural tail with broad dural based CPA mass suggests which tumour?
items.exp: Meningiomas arise from dura showing broad base, dural tail and calcification, often eccentric to meatus. Schwannomas centre on and expand the meatus instead.
r: Incorrect. Schwannoma expands meatus without dural tail.
Correct. Dural tail means meningioma.
Incorrect. Glomus centres on jugular foramen below.
Incorrect. Granuloma is petrous apex blood product lesion.
items.kp: Tail on dura points to meningioma.

items.q: Small asymptomatic vestibular schwannoma in 75 year old most often managed how initially?
o: Watch and wait serial MRI surveillance
items.exp: Many small tumours grow slowly or not at all, so surveillance MRI with intervention only on growth or symptoms spares elderly patients surgical risk. Chemotherapy has no routine role.
r: Incorrect. Surgery risks outweigh in stable elderly disease.
Correct. Serial MRI watch and wait.
Incorrect. No standard chemotherapy exists.
Incorrect. Radiosurgery follows documented growth decisions.
items.kp: Old patient, small stable tumour: scan and watch.

items.q: Glomus jugulare characteristically erodes which skull base structure on CT?
o: Jugular foramen with moth eaten margins
items.exp: Jugulare paragangliomas expand the jugular foramen with irregular moth eaten bone destruction and may invade middle ear from below, unlike tympanicum confined to promontory. Lower cranial nerves suffer as it grows.
r: Incorrect. Tip erosion is mastoiditis pattern.
Correct. Moth eaten jugular foramen.
Incorrect. Oval window is otosclerosis site.
Incorrect. Cribriform is anterior skull base olfactory area.
items.kp: Moth eaten jugular hole equals glomus jugulare.

items.q: Epidermoid cyst of CPA is best distinguished on MRI by what?
items.exp: Keratinaceous epidermoid restricts diffusion brightly unlike CSF following arachnoid cysts, and insinuates around nerves and vessels. It lacks dural base and meatal origin signs.
r: Incorrect. Tail belongs to meningioma.
Correct. Bright diffusion means epidermoid.
Incorrect. Meatal expansion is schwannoma.
Incorrect. Flow voids mark vascular malformations.

items.q: As CPA tumours enlarge beyond cochlear symptoms, which nerve signs appear next classically?
o: Trigeminal sensory loss and reduced corneal reflex
items.exp: Expanding angle masses reach trigeminal nerve in Meckel region causing facial numbness and lost corneal reflex before facial weakness (nerve resists stretch) and later lower cranial or brainstem signs.
r: Incorrect. Optic pathway is distant anterior.
Correct. Trigeminal signs follow cochlear.
Incorrect. Hypoglossal is late lower extension.
Incorrect. Smell is frontal base territory.
items.kp: Numb cheek after deaf ear: tumour growing.

items.q: Chronically discharging ear now with pain, bleeding and facial palsy raises concern for what?
o: Squamous carcinoma of middle ear or canal
items.exp: Malignancy arising in chronic ears changes painless discharge to painful bleeding mass with nerve invasion, needing biopsy (unlike glomus) imaging and radical treatment planning.
r: Incorrect. Flares discharge without bleeding mass and palsy pattern.
Correct. Carcinoma complicating chronic ear.
Incorrect. Wax never paralyses facial nerve.
Incorrect. Effusion has intact drum without discharge.
items.kp: Pain plus blood plus palsy in chronic ear: biopsy for cancer.

items.q: Brown sign in glomus tympanicum examination refers to what?
o: Red mass blanches with pneumatic pressure
items.exp: Pneumatic otoscopy pressure blanches the vascular retrotympanic mass (Brown sign) supporting paraganglioma. It is a gentle diagnostic observation, never biopsy or forceful probing.
r: Incorrect. Perforation is trauma, not this sign.
Correct. Blanching red mass on pressure.
Incorrect. Discharge colour is unrelated sign.
Incorrect. Hearing change is not the sign.
items.kp: Press gently, red fades: Brown sign of glomus.
